name: free forever
description: 42 AI coding tools sorted by how free they really are: 13 free forever, 24 limited, 5 reference. Every number read from the vendor's own page.
license: data is free to quote with attribution to the site

tiers.forever: No card, no expiry. Funded by ads, a vendor, a university or your own hardware.
tiers.limited: A real free allowance that runs out: monthly credits, a one-time grant, an unpublished cap, or a promotion the vendor can end.
tiers.reference: Not tools: directories that probe their own rows, and student bundles that need verification.

evidence.vendor: Read on the company's own page. Their numbers, their words.
evidence.directory: The company did not state it; the figure came from a directory that re-probes its rows on a schedule.

entries.name: freecode
entries.tagline: A coding agent on web, desktop and terminal. Sponsor cards pay the model bill.
entries.free: Free access with a daily usage limit; the site says access resets and tells you when.
entries.howPaid: Sponsor cards are shown in the interface, clearly labelled, and the FAQ says they are “not written into your code”.
catch: The npm installer covers Apple-silicon macOS and Windows x64 only — Intel Macs, Linux and Windows on ARM are out.
Web use asks for GitHub read and write access to your repositories.
The FAQ states session data feeds diagnostics, sponsored recommendations and “eligible data licensing”.
entries.licence: Not stated on the site; the CLI ships on npm as freecode-sh.
entries.why: One of only two here that runs in a browser as well as a terminal, with a start-up guide and an FAQ that names the trade-off instead of hiding it.

entries.name: Freebuff
entries.tagline: The flagship ad-funded agent: CLI, desktop for every OS, browser, Android.
entries.free: 30 hours a day on the free plan — but only in the vendor's 24 “full access” countries. Anywhere else it is 5 hours a day, and 4 over a VPN or proxy. One-hour sessions with unlimited messages; hours reset at midnight in your local timezone and do not roll over.
entries.howPaid: Text ads between agent turns. Paid tiers ($8 / $25 / $60) buy 50, 80 or 130 hours a day and unlock the better models.
catch: The 30 hours is regional. Full access covers the US, Canada, UK, Australia, NZ, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Austria, Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Switzerland, Malta and South Korea; everywhere else the free allowance is 5 hours a day, or 4 on a VPN.

Free runs the two DeepSeek V4.1 Flash variants (15 hrs/day, or 10 on Flash Fast) plus Solar Pro 4 and Solar Mini 4, and Beam 1.0, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and Glyph Cluster, which use none of your hours. GPT-6 Luna, Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Ember, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra are paid-tier models.
The launch post states messages, agent traces, files and usage may be analysed to personalise ads and train ad models.
Hours, not tokens: an hour on a 3x model costs three of your hours.
Full model list differs by country.
entries.why: The widest platform coverage of anything ad-funded — Linux ARM builds and a phone app — and the only one publishing a plain hours table per model.

entries.name: free-pi
entries.tagline: Ad-funded terminal agent with 27 models, including opt-in “Defense” models that will not refuse.
entries.free: A daily allowance set by the server — the limits docs deliberately do not state a number. /usage shows a percentage; a warning appears at 80%.
entries.howPaid: Terminal ad cards; /support opens today's advertiser. An ad partner receives excerpts of your recent conversation to pick the ad.
catch: The consent screen says it plainly: sessions are saved as traces and used to train models, and “they may be shared or sold to third parties” — with no opt-out after accepting.
Alpha, no uptime guarantee, no self-service data deletion.
One active session at a time per account.
Every strong model costs a multiple of the allowance: Kimi K3.1 Pro ~22x, Gemini 4 Neon ~29x, GPT-6.2 Astra ~51x. The Claude and GPT-6.1 models are listed as “temporarily unavailable” right now.
entries.why: Listing this with its own consent text quoted, because that text is the clearest statement of the trade anywhere on this page. Also the only one with a bundled security-audit skill.

entries.name: Tenzy
entries.tagline: Terminal agent built around showing its reasoning, its patches and its test proof.
entries.free: Fair-use budget of 20h 35m of agent time per cycle, resetting every 15 hours. No card to install.
entries.howPaid: Sponsor banners rotate about every 15 seconds; between-turn placements appear after completed work with frequency caps.
catch: Ads are frequent by design: a rotating banner every ~15 seconds while one is visible.
Agent-time accounting, not tokens — cheaper models stretch it, but the clock runs while the agent works.
Default model is DeepSeek V4 Flash; NVIDIA Inkling needs your own key.
The installer shown on the site is PowerShell-first.
entries.why: Publishes the exact allowance (20:35:00, 15-hour reset) and an ad policy that rules out autoplay, fake download buttons and ads touching generated code.

entries.name: VibeFree
entries.tagline: Free AI chat with no login, and the same deal inside a VS Code agent.
entries.free: Guest chat needs no account — an advert pays for each message. An account adds a free daily token allowance and VibeBucks.
entries.howPaid: One ad auction fills every slot; labelled sponsored units appear while the assistant works and beside its replies.
catch: The ad classifier reads the first 1,500 characters of each message you send and keeps topic labels for 30 minutes. The message itself is not kept for ads.
The VS Code extension is a chat panel, not autocomplete.
External ad networks can, with your consent, ask the model to mention a sponsor inside an answer.
Windows desktop app, CLI and standalone IDE are still in development.
entries.licence: Proprietary extension (vibefree.vibefree-vscode). Trading name of TapTapPay Ltd.
entries.why: The only entry here you can use without creating anything, and it documents its ad classifier down to the character count.

entries.name: ADCode
entries.tagline: An AI code editor that pays you: half of eligible ad revenue is credited to you.
entries.free: 140 AI credits a day across included models — roughly 20 agent steps a day, per their own comparison.
entries.howPaid: Sponsored cards. Half of eligible ad revenue is credited to your account; the other half funds the editor. Plans from $19/month raise the allowance.
catch: 20 agent steps a day is a taste, not a working day. Builder ($19) is 85, Pro ($39) is 175, Max ($149) is 661.
Free included AI is one sponsor's models — Tagflow Code 27B and Tagflow Code Flash, sponsored by Tagflow. Heabsy and every other hosted model are pay-as-you-go from credits.
Earnings depend on eligible views and advertiser demand; they are not a wage.
No macOS desktop build yet; the browser version needs a verified account for included AI.
entries.why: The only product here that shares revenue with the user instead of just waiving the bill — and it publishes the step count rather than saying “generous”.

entries.name: Clixad
entries.tagline: Terminal agent with no key and no subscription; free models daily, credits from an offerwall.
entries.free: Seven models free every day up to 60,000 credits of usage per account, inside a daily budget shared by all users; Gemini 3.8 Flash joins them until 15 January 2027. The 25,000-credit signup bonus is gone.
entries.howPaid: Marked terminal ads in up to three places (60-character lines, booked by advertisers by the week) plus surveys and offers completed in a browser tab that convert to credits.
catch: Past the daily limit you pay in credits. Most survey attempts end in a screenout that pays nothing — Clixad's own blog says so.

The free seven are not all budget models — GPT-5 Nano, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and Kimi K2.5 — but everything above them needs earned or bought credits.
Clixad's own funding post says free credits changed after it was written: the signup bonus its worked examples depend on is no longer issued.
Public beta, 18+, shared daily budget so peak hours bite.
The ad network still sees your IP; ad text is chosen by fixed category, never from prompts.
entries.why: Publishes the arithmetic of its own funding, including the parts that are unflattering. `CLIXAD_SPONSOR=0` turns the ads off.

entries.name: Idlen
entries.tagline: Not an agent — an extension that pays you for the time your AI spends thinking.
entries.free: $0 to install. You keep 70% of the ad revenue the wait earns, paid via Stripe, PayPal or as credits.
entries.howPaid: A native sponsored ad shown while the model is working. Advertisers reach you; you take 70% of that revenue.
catch: It earns you money; it does not provide a model. You still bring Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or whatever you already pay for.
Ad relevance is chosen locally from your package.json — the extension says it never reads source code.
Their own earnings calculator (“€20–100/month”) is based on average fill rates, not a promise.
A third-party extension inside your editor — review the code before installing.
entries.licence: Extension code published for security review.
entries.why: A different question from the rest of this page: not “make AI free” but “let the wait pay for some of it”. Worth knowing it exists.

entries.name: idlepay
entries.tagline: Swaps the “thinking…” spinner for one sponsored line. You keep half.
entries.free: Free to install, no card, 50% revenue share, cash out via Stripe past $10.
entries.howPaid: One labelled sponsored line (≤60 characters) replaces the spinner verb during a genuine wait. Clicks pay 50× an impression.
catch: Same as Idlen: it monetises your wait, it does not give you a model.
It reads one timestamp from your Claude session file to tell “coding” from “terminal left open”; everything else stays local.
Uninstall restores your editor settings byte-for-byte — worth verifying yourself, since it does patch your Claude Code config.
Earnings are estimates and depend on live bid prices.
entries.licence: Open-source client, signed marketplace builds, verify.sh against public source.
entries.why: The most aggressively minimal version of the idea — one line, only during a real wait, verifiable builds.

entries.name: Overbrilliant OB-1
entries.tagline: Open Apache-2.0 terminal agent with no account, no card and no key.
entries.free: A built-in free-models router — the project documents 150+ free models across 20+ providers — starts with no key or account; new free models reach free users after 30 days.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free router; paid hosted tier is hard-capped prepaid credits with no overage path.
catch: overbrilliant.com no longer documents the agent at all: the site now sells custom-trained models from $1,500. The free CLI lives on GitHub and npm (@overbrilliant/ob1), with an Apache-2.0 licence and its own README.
New free models lag 30 days behind paying users.
The free router's capacity is whatever the keyless providers choose to give it, so throughput moves around.
Sandboxing is macOS Seatbelt and Linux bubblewrap only.
entries.why: The only entry that needs no account and no key at all, and its README says what the free router actually draws on instead of promising a model tier.

entries.name: opencode
entries.tagline: Open-source agent; its own gateway serves a rotating set of models at zero.
entries.free: Free-tier chat models, usable inside OpenCode with no key or card.
entries.howPaid: The OpenCode Console gateway absorbs the cost; paid models and a Go subscription sit beside it.
catch: The docs state free-tier chat models require OpenCode — you cannot call them from another client.
The free list rotates with provider pricing.
Console sign-in is needed for billing even though the CLI itself runs without an account.
Free models are open-weight, never frontier.
entries.why: The most-installed open agent, with free models wired in rather than bolted on.

entries.name: Google Antigravity
entries.tagline: Agent-first IDE and CLI on a $0 individual plan — with real Claude and Gemini models.
entries.free: $0 plan serving gemini-3.8-flash, claude-opus-4.6, claude-sonnet-4.6 and gpt-oss-120b — all four listed “until 2026-11-30”.
entries.howPaid: Google-funded. No ads at all. Gemini CLI's individual free tier ended 18 June 2026 and Google routes free users here.
catch: Google account required, and Google can change the quota with one announcement — the directory that probes these rows already dates all four models “until 2026-11-30”.
Gemini models and third-party models have separate weekly allowances, and neither amount is published.
Gemini CLI's free tier being switched off is the cautionary tale: vendor free tiers are revocable.
Proprietary and closed source.
entries.why: The strongest free models on this page without watching an ad. Listed as directory-verified because the plan details come from a probed directory, not a page I read.

entries.name: Ollama (local models)
entries.tagline: The only genuinely free-of-strings option: your hardware, your models, no account.
entries.free: Download, pull a model, run it. No key, no account, no card, no telemetry to a vendor.
entries.howPaid: You pay in electricity and hardware. That is the whole business model.
catch: Needs a machine with enough memory — a 27B coding model wants a real GPU, not a Chromebook.
Quality is below frontier models; you are trading capability for independence.
You still need an agent front-end (opencode, Cline, Continue, OB-1) pointed at localhost:11434.
entries.why: Included because every other entry has an asterisk and this one does not. It is the baseline the rest are being measured against.

entries.name: Kilo Code
entries.tagline: Open-source agent for VS Code, JetBrains and the CLI with an Auto Free mode.
entries.free: An Auto Free mode plus a keyless OpenAI-compatible gateway on a handful of free open models.
entries.howPaid: Free models are absorbed by the gateway; 500+ paid models bill through at provider rates.
catch: Auto Free is deliberately the weaker path — mid-size open weights only.
The gateway's free list rotates and can shrink without notice.
One click on a paid model starts billing; easy to drift.
entries.why: Here rather than in the free-forever tier because the free path is a rotating pool, not a standing arrangement.

entries.name: Kiro
entries.tagline: AWS's spec-driven agentic IDE with a perpetual free tier.
entries.free: A perpetual free tier on Claude Sonnet and open-weight models — 50 credits a month, non-rolling, on requests served from the US; successor to Amazon Q Developer.
entries.howPaid: AWS-funded, no ads.
catch: The workflow is opinionated: write requirements before code.
AWS account required.
The free quota is enough to evaluate, not to work in all day.
entries.why: Perpetual rather than promotional, which is why it is not in the “free forever” tier only because the quota is small.

entries.name: Google Jules
entries.tagline: Async cloud agent: hand it a GitHub task and come back to a diff.
entries.free: 15 async tasks per rolling day, 3 at a time, on Gemini models.
entries.howPaid: Google-funded.
catch: Asynchronous only — no real-time steering.
GitHub connection required, with the repository access that implies.
Small daily task count.
entries.why: Good for offloading chores, but the daily cap puts it in this tier.

entries.name: Duck.ai
entries.tagline: Private front-end to six free models with no account at all.
entries.free: Six models signed out: GPT-6 Luna, GPT-5.4 mini, Claude 4.5 Haiku, Mistral Small 4, gpt-oss-120b, Gemma 4 31B.
entries.howPaid: Funded by DuckDuckGo's search business. No ads in the chat.
catch: The daily limit is unpublished, and the big models burn it faster.
Chat only — no files, no repository context.
Chats stay on your device, so nothing follows you between machines.
entries.why: No account and no ads, but an undisclosed cap — the honest description is “limited”.

entries.name: Autohand Code
entries.tagline: Open-source agent for CLI, IDE, browser and mobile with a documented free plan.
entries.free: 15 credits per rolling 5-hour window, up to 100 a month — one credit is one successful hosted response.
entries.howPaid: Hosted Fantail model is vendor-funded; BYOK and local models use no credits at all.
catch: 100 hosted responses a month is roughly three a day.
No card needed, but eligibility is verified: usually a GitHub account at least 30 days old.
The free tier is Fantail only; other models mean your own key.
entries.why: Publishes the full rate-limit matrix on a docs page — rare — but 100 responses a month is a trial in all but name.

entries.name: WorkBuddy
entries.tagline: IDE and CLI agent with a credit-based free plan and a heavy promotional period.
entries.free: 100 credits a month, 5,000 code completions a month, 3 automated tasks — plus a limited-time promo of 30 credits a day.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free plan; Pro at $10/month ($7 first month) buys 2,000 credits and unlimited completions.
catch: The good numbers are promotional and the docs say plainly they will not always be available.
100 base credits a month is almost nothing once the promo ends.
Credits are monthly and do not roll over.
entries.why: Listed because its docs separate base credits from promo credits — most products blur the two.

entries.name: DeepAI
entries.tagline: Free plan for chat, images and its DeepAI Code desktop app. API is paid.
entries.free: Limited HD images and editing, limited standard chat, up to 250 “Theos” a day in DeepAI Code, 60s/day of voice chat.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free tier with an ad-supported free experience; Pro at $9.99/month (or $7.50 annual) removes ads and raises everything.
catch: Free chat is limited to Standard models. Genius and Super Genius — GPT-6.2 Sol, Grok 4.3, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.2 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon — are Pro only.
The API is not free at all: the docs state API access requires a DeepAI Pro subscription.
Theos are a daily allowance, not a durable pool.
entries.why: Worth including to kill a common assumption: DeepAI's free tier does not extend to its API, which its own docs say is Pro-only.

entries.name: Cursor (Hobby)
entries.tagline: The best-known AI editor; its free plan is small and clearly a funnel.
entries.free: A limited free allotment of agent requests and completions on the Hobby plan.
entries.howPaid: Subscription from $20/month; the free plan is product-led acquisition.
catch: The free quota lasts a short session, not a week of work.
The best models are behind the paid plans.
Account required.
entries.why: Included as a calibration point: this is what the industry calls “a free plan” when the aim is conversion.

entries.name: TRAE (TraeCode)
entries.tagline: ByteDance's AI IDE with a one-time basic allowance.
entries.free: Auto mode only on the free plan, plus a one-time Basic usage allowance and limited autocompletion.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded promotional tiers.
catch: Auto mode means you do not choose the model.
The allowance is one-time, not monthly.
Proprietary, and data terms worth reading before using work code.
entries.why: A large free headline that is really a one-shot trial — exactly the shape this tier is here to flag.

entries.name: Qoder
entries.tagline: Alibaba's coding apps with a free basic-model allowance and daily promotional credits.
entries.free: Ongoing free basic-model allowance, a Qwen promotion, a 300-credit Pro trial and daily credits to claim.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded promotional tiers.
catch: A stack of promotions that each expire separately.
The best models sit behind the Pro trial, which ends.
Account required.
entries.why: The free tier is really four overlapping promotions — a good example of why this tier exists separately.

entries.name: GitHub Copilot Free
entries.tagline: The default free plan most people already have by accident.
entries.free: A free individual plan: 2,000 completions a month plus a chat and agent allowance GitHub does not put a number on.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free tier; paid plans from $10.
catch: Monthly completions and chat requests run out quickly once an agent is involved.
Free sign-ups have been paused and reopened at various points — availability has changed before.
GitHub account required.
entries.why: Usually already available to you, which makes it the free tier most people should try before installing anything else.

entries.name: Codex (ChatGPT Free)
entries.tagline: Codex access on a $0 ChatGPT plan, where the rollout allows it.
entries.free: Codex on the Free plan, subject to rollout; unlimited text chat with GPT-6 Luna.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded; Plus at $20/month.
catch: The free allowance is not published — OpenAI does not state a number.
Rollout varies by country and account.
ChatGPT account required.
entries.why: Genuinely usable for small tasks, but “unpublished allowance” is the whole problem with vendor free tiers.

entries.name: Macaly
entries.tagline: Chat-to-website builder with a real free plan: one published app, 1M credits a month.
entries.free: 1 published app on a Macaly domain, 1M monthly credits, limited usage through ChatGPT and Claude.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free plan; Starter $10/month unlocks custom domains.
catch: One published app only, and no custom domain until you pay.
Monthly credits, not a daily drip.
An app builder, not a code editor for an existing repository.
entries.why: The most usable “free forever” app builder of the ones I read, because 1M monthly credits is a real number rather than a countdown.

entries.name: bolt.new
entries.tagline: Browser app builder with a token allowance and free hosting.
entries.free: A monthly token allowance on the free plan, public and private projects, website hosting.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free tier; paid from $25/month.
catch: Token allowance is spent fast by a real build.
The free tier is aimed at trying the product.
Switching between many tools on one project gets awkward.
entries.licence: Proprietary (bolt.diy is the MIT open-source fork).
entries.why: Included for the browser-builder category; bolt.diy is the free-forever route if you want it open source.

entries.name: Google AI Studio (Gemini API)
entries.tagline: Free Gemini API keys with per-model rate limits, no card.
entries.free: A free tier on the Gemini API — Gemini 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash, Gemma 4 and others.
entries.howPaid: Google-funded free tier; pay-as-you-go above it.
catch: Free-tier prompts may be used to improve Google's products — never paste secrets.
Rate limits are per model and change with announcements.
A key plus a client is needed; this is not an agent on its own.
entries.why: The default free key behind half the open agents on this page.

entries.name: Groq
entries.tagline: Very fast inference on a free plan with a published per-model rate table.
entries.free: Free plan on gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b and Qwen 3.8 27B with published limits.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free tier; paid on-demand beside it.
catch: Open-weight models only, and the roster churns.
Rate limits are strict enough that agents need retry logic.
Key required.
entries.why: When latency is the problem — tight test loops, autocomplete — this is the fastest free inference available.

entries.name: NVIDIA NIM
entries.tagline: Free endpoints for open models at build.nvidia.com with a developer key.
entries.free: Free endpoints on models NVIDIA marks “Free Endpoint”, including GLM, Nemotron, Gemma and gpt-oss.
entries.howPaid: NVIDIA-funded for as long as the programme runs.
catch: Needs an NVIDIA Developer account and key.
Only models marked Free Endpoint qualify.
Shared capacity can be slow at peak.
entries.why: The widest free catalogue of respectable open weights.

entries.name: OpenRouter
entries.tagline: One key for a rotating set of zero-priced models, plus a free router.
entries.free: Models priced at zero, and an `openrouter/free` router that picks one at random for each request.
entries.howPaid: Providers and paid traffic subsidise the free pool.
catch: Free models are rate-limited and heavily used.
Some free routes log prompts for training — read each model card.
The free list rotates constantly; the router may pick a weaker model than you expected.
entries.why: The single key that drops into nearly every agent here as BYOK, with no card.

entries.name: FreeInference (Harvard SEAS)
entries.tagline: A university lab serving open models free, including an Anthropic-shaped endpoint.
entries.free: Free open models — DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash, MiniMax M3, Qwen 3.6 — over OpenAI and Anthropic-shaped endpoints.
entries.howPaid: University research project.
catch: Research capacity: uptime is best-effort and it could stop without notice.
The Anthropic-shaped endpoint slots into Claude Code but is not an officially supported pairing.
Prompts and responses may be logged for research, and sanitised content and usage statistics may be published. It is a lab experiment, not a privacy product.
Key required.
entries.why: The only free endpoint that speaks Anthropic's protocol, so existing Claude Code habits carry over.

entries.name: LLM7.io
entries.tagline: OpenAI-compatible API with a recurring daily token allowance.
entries.free: 100,000 input plus output tokens a day on eligible turbo models.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free tier.
catch: The daily allowance is small for agent work.
Turbo models are the cheap tier.
Key required.
entries.why: One of the few that publishes a real recurring number instead of “generous limits”.

entries.name: OVHcloud AI Endpoints
entries.tagline: EU-hosted open models, anonymous: no signup, no key, no card.
entries.free: Anonymous OpenAI-compatible calls to gpt-oss-120b, Qwen 3.6 and Qwen 3.8 27B.
entries.howPaid: OVHcloud-funded.
catch: Anonymous means shared limits and no support.
Small catalogue.
Data residency in the EU — the point for some users.
entries.why: The only zero-signup, zero-key API on this page.

entries.name: Z.ai (Zhipu GLM)
entries.tagline: GLM Flash models free on the API, vision included.
entries.free: GLM 4.7 Flash, 4.5 Flash and 4.6V Flash at zero price.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded.
catch: Flash only — the large GLMs are paid.
Chinese provider: read the data terms.
Key required.
entries.why: A free Flash model with vision, which is rare and useful for screenshot-to-code.

entries.name: Cloudflare Workers AI
entries.tagline: Serverless inference on a daily free allowance, right next to your Worker.
entries.free: A daily free allowance of “neurons” across hosted open models.
entries.howPaid: Vendor-funded free allowance.
catch: Best used inside Workers, so it needs a Cloudflare account and a deploy step.
The allowance is small and per account.
Open models only.
entries.why: Free inference that ships with the code it serves, with no separate provider account.

entries.name: Pollinations.AI
entries.tagline: Text and image generation with no signup and no key at all.
entries.free: An anonymous legacy text endpoint on text.pollinations.ai (gpt-oss-20b). The current gen.pollinations.ai API needs a key and bills Pollen credits.
entries.howPaid: Community-funded free service.
catch: The text endpoint is labelled “legacy”.
One small model.
Shared queue, slow at peak.
entries.why: The fastest way to prove an idea without creating an account — images included.

entries.name: awesome-free-ai-coding
entries.tagline: 118 live free offers, probe-verified twice a week, with the evidence linked.
entries.free: MIT licensed. No tracking, no ads, no affiliate links.
entries.howPaid: Volunteer project; GitHub Actions probe every row twice a week and archive offers after three failed probes.
catch: It is a list — you still wire everything up.
Ended offers can linger until the next probe.
Very broad: easy to disappear into.
entries.why: The best place to check whether a free tier still exists this week, because every row links its proof.

entries.name: freellm.site
entries.tagline: 74 providers with free tiers, each row saying whether a card is required.
entries.free: Free to read; 29 providers marked “always free”.
entries.howPaid: A plain directory, last updated 2026-09-29, with a verification column.
catch: Rows go stale between updates.
“Free credits on signup” is not “free forever” — read the column.
It lists; it does not test.
entries.why: Good breadth when you need a free key for a specific model and want the card requirement in the same row.

entries.name: VibeLedger free-tools index
entries.tagline: 88 free options with each vendor's free-plan wording quoted.
entries.free: Free to read; checked 31 October 2026.
entries.howPaid: Editorial tracker, no ads.
catch: Quotes vendors rather than testing them.
Some entries were “verified” without the exact limits being captured.
Checked 31 October 2026 — 26 days before this re-check.
entries.why: Useful because it prints the vendor's own sentence instead of a summary of it.

entries.name: GitHub Student Developer Pack
entries.tagline: Around 80 partner offers for verified students, from one verification.
entries.free: Cloud credit, JetBrains IDEs, domains and more, donated by partners.
entries.howPaid: Companies donate to win student loyalty.
catch: Needs student verification and age 13+.
Offers expire and change; several closed during 2026.
Each partner's terms still apply.
entries.why: The highest-value free bundle on this page, if you are eligible.

entries.name: Azure for Students
entries.tagline: $100 of credit a year plus free services, no credit card.
entries.free: $100 credit per year, renewable while enrolled.
entries.howPaid: Microsoft-funded for full-time university students.
catch: Full-time university students only, verified.
Credit does not roll over, and overages stop services.
Azure's pricing is not cheap.
entries.why: Enough to host a real side project — and an AI endpoint — for a year without a card.
